links.outcome: Performance variation across prompt strategies and prompt language on Chinese clinical text
links.effect: English prompts gave mean F1 61.38% vs Chinese prompts 56.65% on balanced subset; CoT prompting helped MetS but was largely detrimental for DKD.
links.quote: Furthermore, the analysis revealed a clear language bias, with English prompts yielding a superior mean F1-score (61.38%) compared to Chinese prompts (56.65%) across all models ( Supplementary Figure 6 and Supplementary Figure 7 in the Supplementary Figures ).

links.outcome: LLM diagnostic performance on real-world clinical narratives versus rule-based tasks
links.effect: Peak F1 0.951 for diabetes subtyping but only 0.570 for DKD and 0.650 for MetS diagnosis from real-world discharge summaries.
links.quote: In the diabetes classification task (Task 1), the DeepSeek-V3 model with Chinese Prompt 1 achieved the best F1 score of 0.951.

links.outcome: Model performance on non-English (Chinese) clinical text by prompt language
links.effect: English prompts outperformed Chinese prompts on native Chinese clinical text (mean F1 61.38% vs 56.65%); MMedLM2-7B had poor English generalization (F1 0.697).
links.quote: A consistent and critical finding was the superior performance of English prompts on Chinese clinical text, highlighting the Anglocentric bias of many foundational models.

links.outcome: Performance on minority diabetes subtype classes
links.effect: Top model misclassified 61% of GDM and 42% of SD cases as T2DM; balanced-subset F1 peaked at 77.39% vs 0.951 on imbalanced data.
links.quote: A confusion matrix analysis revealed the top-performing model (DeepSeek-V3, Chinese Prompt 1) suffered from significant class imbalance, misclassifying high proportions of minority classes like GDM (61%) and SD (42%) as T2DM.

links.outcome: LLM hallucination and reasoning errors in rule-based diagnosis
links.effect: In 0.83% of cases with absent indicators the model still generated a positive DKD diagnosis; 49.77% of MetS cases self-identified as meeting ≥3 criteria were misclassified.
links.quote: Furthermore, even when at least one indicator was successfully extracted, the diagnostic error rate remained at 27.02%.

links.outcome: missing diagnostic indicators in DKD failures
links.effect: Overall UACR/AER missingness was 64.19%/59.36%; among incorrect DKD predictions, UACR/AER missingness was 52.01%/46.09%, both absent in 24.13%.
links.quote: Specifically, within incorrectly predicted cases, UACR and AER were missing in 52.01% and 46.09% of instances, with both completely absent in 24.13% of failures ( Supplementary Figure 18A ).

links.effect: 0.83% of cases with entirely absent indicators still received positive DKD diagnoses; MetS logic errors included 49.77% and 21.94% inconsistency rates.
links.quote: While this widespread missingness frequently forced the model into a default “conservative” negative prediction, the explicit extraction exposed a critical “hallucination” vulnerability: in 0.83% of cases where diagnostic indicators were entirely absent, the model still baselessly generated a positive diagnosis.
Conversely, the models exhibited brittle performance on DKD and MetS tasks, revealing a core limitation in executing procedural rules that demand strict quantitative and logical adherence.
